title: My First Internship: What I Expected vs What I Found
paragraphs: Before I started my internship at DataBridge Solutions in Astana, I had a clear picture in my head of what it would be like. I would sit at a sleek desk in a modern office, write elegant code, attend important meetings, and gradually build something real. The reality was somewhat different — but, in the end, far more valuable than the fantasy.

The first shock was the pace. I had expected a gentle introduction — perhaps a week of orientation, some training sessions, then gradually increasing responsibility. Instead, on day two, I was assigned to a team that was already deep into a project, handed a codebase I had never seen, and told that my task was to fix a bug affecting the payment system. I had been studying computer science for two years. I had never worked on a real payment system before. The bug took me three days to find and fix — but I found it.

The second discovery was about communication. In my courses, the emphasis had always been on the product: write good code, solve the problem, produce the solution. In the workplace, I quickly discovered that how you communicate about what you are doing is almost as important as doing it. I had to write progress updates for my supervisor, explain technical issues to non-technical colleagues, and present my work in a team meeting. My English improved more in six weeks than in a previous year of study.

The third discovery was about mistakes. I made several — some embarrassing, one quite serious. I deleted a file I should not have deleted and spent an entire afternoon recovering it. My supervisor was not angry. She told me: "The only way to never make mistakes is to never try anything difficult. Keep going." This was more useful than any lecture.

I had been working at DataBridge for about four weeks when I realised something had shifted. I was no longer arriving at the office thinking about what I would learn that day. I was arriving thinking about what I needed to do — and how to do it well. That shift — from student to worker — was the most important thing the internship taught me.

Six weeks passed quickly. On my last day, the team gave me feedback in a formal session. They said I had improved significantly in my communication, shown real initiative in the later weeks, and delivered work that was "good enough for production" — the highest praise a junior developer can receive. I had been preparing for this feedback for days. When I heard it, I felt something I had not expected: I wanted to come back.

If I were to give one piece of advice to a student about to start their first internship, it would be this: go in with no expectations, and be ready to be surprised — in every direction. The internship will not be what you imagine. It will be better. And harder. And more real.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Amir, you've been really quiet since you came back from the internship. Was it good?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: It was incredible. And very hard. I've been thinking about it every day since.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: How much communication matters. I spent as much time writing updates as writing code.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Has it changed how you study here at WKU?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Completely. I've started thinking about every assignment as a workplace problem, not a test.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: That sounds like a big shift. Are you going to apply for the same company next year?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I've been looking at their website every day since I came home. So yes — probably.

keyPhrases.context: "A week of orientation." = introductory period when you learn how things work.
"A codebase I had never seen." = the full body of code for a project.
"Write progress updates for my supervisor." — regular reports on what you've done.
"Shown real initiative." = acting independently and making your own decisions.
"Good enough for production." = code that can go into the live, real system.
"A formal feedback session." = a structured meeting to discuss your performance.
"That shift — from student to worker." = a change in mindset or identity.
"Junior developer." = entry-level programmer in a tech company.

vocab.definition: an introductory period helping someone learn about a new situation
vocab.example: "A week of orientation, then gradually increasing responsibility."

vocab.definition: the ability to assess situations and act without being told
vocab.example: "Shown real initiative in the later weeks." — acting on your own without being asked.

vocab.definition: in tech: the live system used by real customers
vocab.example: "Good enough for production" — the code can go into the real, working system.

vocab.definition: a person who oversees and manages others' work
vocab.example: "Write progress updates for my supervisor." — the person above you who checks your work.
"Write elegant code." — code that is clean, efficient, and easy to read.

vocab.definition: to give special importance to something
vocab.example: "Courses had always emphasised the product." — focused on delivering the solution.

vocab.definition: to get something back; to restore something to its original state
vocab.example: "Spent an afternoon recovering it." = restoring the deleted file.
"Gradually increasing responsibility." = more and more, bit by bit.
